extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; policymakers and educated public interested in political economy
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for judging economic systems, policies, and the productive character of different classes of labour, with examples and historical comparisons. Focuses on how division of labour, saving, trade, and government policy affect a nation's real annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of productive and unproductive labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Productive labour includes artificers, manufacturers, and merchants; menial servants are classed among the barren or unproductive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith distinguishes labour that adds to the annual produce of land and labour (productive) from labour that merely consumes revenue (unproductive). This classification is used to evaluate the economic contribution of different occupations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produced value adds to real annual revenue even when consumption equals production
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if the consumption of a class equals its production over a period, their labour may still increase the real revenue (annual produce) because the work they produce is exchangeable and adds to the quantity/value of goods available over the year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: an artificer who produces ten pounds' worth of work in six months while consuming ten pounds' worth of corn actually adds ten pounds to the annual produce because his produced work can purchase a half-yearly revenue; thus the value of consumption+production for the period is twenty pounds rather than ten. The argument rebuts assertions that production equal to consumption implies no net contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parsimony and saving increase capital and thereby augment useful labour
rubrics_metrics.description: The increase in the quantity of useful labour employed in a society depends on the increase of the capital which employs it, and that increase must equal savings from revenue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If merchants, artificers, and manufacturers are more inclined to saving than proprietors and cultivators, they are more likely to increase useful labour and thereby increase real revenue. Policy evaluation should consider classes' propensities to save and invest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capacity for division of labour and machinery determines potential productivity improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: Improvements in productive powers depend on the workman's ability and on the machinery; labour that can be more subdivided (manufacturing) is capable of greater improvement than agricultural labour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because manufacturing labour can be reduced to simpler operations and subdivided more, it can benefit more from skill improvements and machinery. This criterion favors industries amenable to division of labour when assessing where productivity gains are likely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign trade and manufactures increase a country's available subsistence
rubrics_metrics.description: A trading and manufacturing country can annually import a greater quantity of subsistence than its own lands could afford in their current state; small quantities of manufactured goods can purchase large quantities of rude produce abroad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: towns draw from the country the rude produce and export manufactured produce; a small part of manufactured produce can buy a great amount of rude produce of other countries. Hence trade and manufactures, other things equal, raise inhabitants' subsistence and living standards compared to a country without trade.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extent of the market regulates the degree of division of labour and manufacturing perfection
rubrics_metrics.description: The degree to which the division of labour can be introduced into any manufacture is necessarily regulated by the extent of the market; larger home/foreign markets permit greater subdivision and perfection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: China's vast home market and internal water carriage allow considerable subdivision of labour and manufacturing; smaller or confined markets limit how far division of labour can be applied and thus constrain manufacturing development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies of restraint or artificial preference are counterproductive to national wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that either draw extraordinary capital toward a particular industry by encouragements or withdraw capital by restraints are subversive of the society's progress toward real wealth; they retard rather than accelerate growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: agricultural systems that restrain manufactures to favor agriculture ultimately discourage agriculture itself; mercantile encouragements may shift capital to less advantageous industries. Smith argues for natural liberty—minimal interference—so individuals can pursue interest freely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural liberty: limited sovereign duties
rubrics_metrics.description: Under the system of natural liberty, the sovereign has only three duties: (1) protection from foreign violence and invasion, (2) protecting members from injustice (administration of justice), and (3) erecting and maintaining certain public works and institutions not profitable for individuals to provide.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Government should avoid attempting to superintend private industry; its proper functions are narrow and intelligible. Evaluation of policy should judge whether government actions fall within these duties or improperly direct private industry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public expenditure must be financed and allocated sensibly
rubrics_metrics.description: The proper performance of the sovereign's duties requires expense, which requires revenue; one must decide which expenses should be defrayed by the whole society or by particular parts, which methods should be used for contributions, and the effects of government borrowing on real wealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith previews analysis of what public expenses are necessary, how society may contribute, and the causes/effects of public debt. This establishes fiscal policy criteria: fairness of burden, choice of taxation methods, and prudence regarding debt's impact on annual produce.

rubrics_metrics.name: Free labour and absence of caste/slavery encourage invention and lower production costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Systems that confine people to castes or employ slaves discourage invention and the use of machinery; freemen are the inventors of improvements in machinery and methods, so slave-based or caste-based labour tends to make manufacture dearer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical examples: Roman and Greek economies had many trades performed by slaves, which limited invention and made some manufactures excessively dear. Evaluations of institutional arrangements should consider their effect on incentives to innovate and adopt machinery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative prices of manufactured versus rude produce affect agricultural incentives
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever tends to raise the price of manufactured produce tends to lower the price of the crude produce of the land, thereby discouraging agriculture; the smaller the quantity of manufactured produce purchased by a given quantity of rude produce, the less encouragement for landlords and farmers to improve or cultivate land.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy that raises manufactured goods' prices or reduces number of artificers/manufacturers diminishes the home market for agricultural produce and thus discourages investment in agriculture. Evaluation of price effects across sectors is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Openness to foreign trade facilitates technological transfer and manufacturing improvement
rubrics_metrics.description: A more extensive navigation and foreign trade would allow countries (e.g., China) to learn and adopt machines and other improvements from other nations, thereby increasing productive powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Smith argues that confinement of foreign trade limits opportunities to learn arts and construct machines used elsewhere; thus policy restricting foreign trade should be evaluated for its long-term effects on technological diffusion and productivity.
